findings.claim: Knowledge check [3]: “Darcy proposes by telling Elizabeth he loves her ‘against my will, against my _____, and even against my character.’”
findings.truth: The words are Elizabeth’s, not Darcy’s. In her rebuttal she asks why he “chose to tell me that you liked me against your will, against your reason, and even against your character”. Darcy’s own proposal opens “In vain have I struggled.” The lesson’s own content_html states this correction two blocks earlier, so the knowledge check contradicts its own lesson.
findings.evidence: Gutenberg #1342 ch. 34 (line 7591): “...you chose to tell me that you liked me against your will, against your reason, and even against your character?”; ch. 34 (line 7536) “In vain have I struggled.”

findings.claim: Flashcard [12]: “Which devastating Darcy line from the FIRST proposal shows his initial pride?” → “‘Against my will, against my reason, and even against my character.’”
findings.truth: Same misattribution as F1. The line is Elizabeth’s, spoken back at Darcy in the second person (“against your will…”). The lesson’s own collapsible n8 flags this, so the flashcard teaches the error the lesson corrects.
findings.evidence: Gutenberg #1342 ch. 34, line 7591. “against my will” does not appear anywhere in the novel.

findings.claim: “Analyse the language shift from pride (‘against my will’) to humility (‘have your feelings changed?’).”
findings.truth: Both quoted phrases are wrong. ‘against my will’ is Elizabeth’s (F1). ‘have your feelings changed?’ is not in the novel; Darcy’s second proposal says “If your feelings are still what they were last April, tell me so at once. My affections and wishes are unchanged.”

findings.claim: Practice question [2] mark scheme: “Analyses Darcy’s language (‘against my will’)”.
findings.truth: Same misattribution as F1; the mark scheme would reward a wrong attribution. Replaced with Darcy’s real opening line.

findings.claim: Practice question [1] mark scheme: “Analyses the shift from dialogue (‘against my will’) to action (secret rescue)”.

Elizabeth’s key quotation is given throughout the unit as “How despicably I have acted!” — in L3 (content_html ×2, conclusion_html, exam_tip_html, the printed extract in practice question [0], knowledge check [2], flashcard [12], glossary), L6 (content_html ×2, knowledge check [2], flashcard [0]) and L7 (content_html ×2, flashcard [2]).
findings.truth: Austen writes “How despicably have I acted!” — verb before subject. This is the unit’s most-repeated quotation and it is printed as an exam extract, so students memorise the wrong word order. In L3 content_html the quotation also splices two non-adjacent sentences; an ellipsis now marks the cut.
findings.evidence: Gutenberg #1342 ch. 36, line 8136: “‘How despicably have I acted!’ she cried. ‘I, who have prided myself on my discernment! I, who have valued myself on my abilities! … How humiliating is this discovery!’”

findings.claim: Mrs Reynolds: “I have never known a cross word from him in my life.” (also flashcard [3]).
findings.truth: She says “had”, not “known”: “I have never had a cross word from him in my life”.

findings.claim: Key fact: Darcy secretly rescues Lydia, and “For Elizabeth, discovering this transforms her understanding completely: ‘Such a change in a man of so much pride excited not only astonishment but gratitude.’”
findings.truth: That sentence is in ch. 44 and describes Elizabeth’s feelings about Darcy’s changed manner during the Pemberley and Lambton visit. It comes before Lydia’s elopement (ch. 46) and long before Elizabeth learns of the rescue (ch. 52). Quoting it as her reaction to the rescue puts it at the wrong point in the plot.
findings.evidence: Gutenberg #1342 ch. 44, line 10054 (ch. 44 runs lines 9851–10087); ch. 46 begins line 10273; the rescue is revealed in ch. 52.

findings.claim: “Elizabeth admits: ‘My feelings are so different from what they were… that I receive your assurances with pleasure and gratitude.’”
findings.truth: Fabricated quotation. Austen never gives Elizabeth’s acceptance in direct speech. The narrator reports it: she “gave him to understand that her sentiments had undergone so material a change since the period to which he alluded, as to make her receive with gratitude and pleasure his present assurances”. A student quoting the lesson’s version would be quoting words that are not in the novel.

findings.claim: Flashcard [10]: “Where does Darcy first ask Elizabeth to dance?” → “At the Netherfield ball.”
findings.truth: Darcy first asks for Elizabeth’s hand at Sir William Lucas’s party in ch. 6, and she refuses; he also invites her to dance a reel at Netherfield in ch. 10. The Netherfield ball (ch. 18) is where she first dances with him. Question reworded so the taught answer is correct.
findings.evidence: Gutenberg #1342 ch. 6, line 1615 (“Mr. Darcy, with grave propriety, requested to be allowed the honour of her hand, but in vain”); ch. 10, line 2603; ch. 18, line 4042.

findings.claim: In every lesson only practice question [0] prints an extract; questions [1]–[5] are whole-text essays labelled “30 marks — 19th Century Essay”.
findings.truth: AQA 8702 Paper 1 Section B always prints an extract and asks students to write about the extract and then the novel as a whole. The marks (30) and the AO split (AO1 12 / AO2 12 / AO3 6, no SPaG) are correct throughout the unit, and whole-text prompts are useful revision practice, so this is recorded rather than edited.
findings.evidence: specs/aqa/english-literature-8702-8702.md, Paper 1 Questions: “Section B The 19th-century novel… required to write in detail about an extract from the novel and then to write about the novel as a whole.” Paper 1 = 64 marks (34 Shakespeare incl. 4 SPaG + 30 novel).

findings.claim: Charlotte is quoted as “I am not romantic, you know; I never was.” (L1 content_html and flashcard, L7 quotation bank); the opening line is quoted with a comma after “fortune”.
findings.truth: Gutenberg prints a full stop, not a semicolon: “I am not romantic, you know. I never was.” The comma after “fortune” is a real first-edition variant. Both are punctuation only, no wording is wrong, and no mark turns on them.

summary: Six lessons carry at least one real error. Three clusters dominate: the phrase “against my will, against my reason, and even against my character” is repeatedly given to Darcy when it is Elizabeth’s rebuttal (the lessons’ own prose says so); Elizabeth’s key quotation is printed unit-wide as “How despicably I have acted!” instead of “How despicably have I acted!”, including inside a printed exam extract; and L5 puts a fabricated direct quotation in Elizabeth’s mouth at the second proposal, which Austen writes only in reported speech. All exam claims (30 marks, AO1 12 / AO2 12 / AO3 6, no SPaG on Section B) match the spec.
